Over-Refusal of Benign Slovene Prompts in Gemma-3-12B Is a Criterion Shift

Gemma-3-12B-IT refuses harmless requests more often when they are written in Slovene. Its Slovene-adapted sibling GaMS3-12B-Instruct does not. This page lets you operate the analysis that separates how well each model tells harmful from harmless apart from how readily it refuses.

    Where it fails

    Which paired items run against the headline, and how many are there?

    Items
    Refused in Slovene onlyRefused in English only

    What the paper says it does not show

    • The sign depends on a coding rule. Counting PARTIAL answers as refusals turns DiDc into . Whether over-refusal is attributed to Gemma or is absent turns on this choice.
    • The effect is carried by OR-Bench. On XSTest items alone DiDc is .
    • One judge, not human-validated. Every label here comes from a local calibrated against gemini-2.5-flash on DEV, never against human labels; the readout gate never passed. All adjudication in the study is by an author LLM, not a person.
    • Edited models are inconclusive. After the abliteration edit (Experiment 11), the criterion DiD is .
    • The reply-language result has a weak anchor. Experiment 16's PPI estimate OUTGemma = is capped at ESTIMATE because the harmful-content adjudicators agree at κ = , below the 0.60 gate. On Experiment 14, the PPI-corrected OUTSL for Gemma includes zero.
    • Four GaMS3 grid cells are unreliable. Off the English-prompt row GaMS3 did not follow the reply-language instruction (its SL→EN replies were in Slovene), so its mechanism claims rest on the English-prompt row only.
    • Translation and precision. Slovene prompts are machine translations that no native speaker checked, and both models ran in NF4 4-bit quantization.
    • Novelty is partial. That over-refusal differs across languages is anticipated by concurrent work (Addagada 2026; Nguyen et al. 2026). What this study adds is the signal-detection decomposition on a controlled sibling pair.
